title: The Long Way Up: Neumann's First Trophy, Led From the Front
title_candidates: The Long Way Up: Neumann's First Trophy, Led From the Front
Sixth, Fifth, Third, Second — First: Neumann Finally Gets There
Two Spoons and a Trophy: Neumann Never Gives Up the Lead
Records at Both Ends: Neumann Wins, Estoril Suffers
theme: A man whose TEG cabinet contained two Wooden Spoons and nothing else takes the lead on the first afternoon at Oitavos and is never headed — while around him the Lisbon Coast surrenders course records at both the brilliant and the catastrophic end of the register.
opening_hook: Open on Stuart Neumann's honours board before this TEG — two Wooden Spoons, no Trophy, and a finishing sequence reading 6th, 5th, 3rd, 2nd — then cut straight to the leaderboard after R1 at Oitavos Dunes, which he topped by 5 and never left. Non-chronological because the climb, not the R1 exchanges, is the story.

trophy_storyline.subject: Stuart Neumann's first Trophy — 156 points, led after every single round
trophy_storyline.why_it_matters: Neumann arrived with no prior Trophy wins and two prior Wooden Spoons, and with last-four finishes of 6th, 5th, 3rd and 2nd; the last rung of that ladder was the only one left.
trophy_storyline.shape: He opened with 39 points at Oitavos Dunes for a lead of 5 (b43 records the same order after R2, b28 after R3, b08 after R4 — the leaderboard's top line never changed), and the two lead changes all TEG came on holes 4 and 5 of the very first round, before anyone had settled. He was best in the field in R1, R2 and R3 and the margin simply widened — 5, then 7, then 12 — and at Estoril he signed off with 43 points and a 92 gross, a personal best at the course by 14 shots. He was not tidy about it: a quintuple-bogey 9 at Estoril's 8th, stroke index 1 (b46), cost him nothing, because he beat Gregg Williams head-to-head in all four rounds and finished 13 clear (b01).

jacket_storyline.subject: Gregg Williams retains the Green Jacket at +66, by 16 — best gross in the field in all four rounds
jacket_storyline.why_it_matters: Williams came in as defending Trophy champion with only 1 prior Jacket win to his name; he loses the Trophy by 13 and keeps the Jacket by 16, and b02's context ranks the +66 fifth all-time.
jacket_storyline.shape: He led the gross from R1 (89 at Oitavos, a personal best there by 2) but only by 3, and Jon Baker drew level twice during R2 at Troia while Williams was busy going four holes without a net par from the 8th (b41) and dropping six shots across 13-15 (b50). Penha Longa in R3 settled it: after a triple at the 3rd and a double at the 4th he birdied the 5th to stop the bleeding (b25), then went five holes from the 11th without dropping a gross shot (b18) and banked nine points across 13-15 (b23) — 87 gross, and the lead went from 4 to 14. R4 at Estoril brought his second course personal best of the TEG, 80, though even that ended in farce: the steady run of pars broke with a double at the 9th (b06) and a quadruple-bogey 8 at the 14th (b03). Not smooth — just reliably better than everyone else with a scorecard in their hand.

spoon_storyline.subject: Alex Baker takes back-to-back Wooden Spoons on 127 points — bottom of the table from the first round to the last
spoon_storyline.why_it_matters: He was the reigning Spoon holder from TEG 15 and already had 2 prior Spoons; this makes three, and he set new course-worst records at two different venues on the way.
spoon_storyline.shape: It was effectively gone on day one: 113 gross at Oitavos Dunes, a new course-worst across 12 prior visits (cr03), built on quintuple bogeys at the 1st and 11th and a sextuple-bogey 10 at the 17th (b37), with 11 shots bled over the closing three holes. He dropped outright to the bottom of the Spoon race for the last time at Troia's 13th in R2 and stayed there, having shed 13 shots between the 13th and 17th (b33). The Estoril finale was the fitting full stop — 107 gross, another course-worst (cr02), 14 shots leaked between the 5th and the 10th (b30), a 9 at the 1st (b32) and a septuple-bogey 11 at the 12th (b09) — 127 points all in, four adrift of his own brother (b24).

discovered_storylines.subject: Estoril, R4: David Mullin turns 30 points into 45 and takes the course record with him
discovered_storylines.why_it_matters: Mullin holds 9 prior Jacket wins and had just posted his worst round of the TEG; his answer was an 80 at Estoril, a new course record beating the previous 86 across 6 prior visits, and his own personal best there by 14.
discovered_storylines.shape: Penha Longa in R3 had been a mess — 98 gross, 13 shots worse than his last visit there, capped by a quadruple-bogey 8 at the 16th, stroke index 1 (b05) — and only two clean closing holes (b29) saved anything at all. At Estoril he birdied the 2nd, paired it with the 3rd (b22), stopped a bogey run with a birdie at the 7th (b04), then piled up 9 points from the 11th to the 13th (b07) and parred the 16th and 17th (b10) for 80 gross and 45 points, a 15-point swing on the previous day (b13, cr01). The same course, the same afternoon, also produced Alex Baker's 107 (cr02) — 27 shots between the new record and the new course-worst.

discovered_storylines.subject: The 12th hole and the Baker brothers
discovered_storylines.why_it_matters: Alex and Jon Baker are brothers, and between them they made the 12th the most expensive hole of the TEG — twice on a par 5 that Penha Longa rates stroke index 17, the second-easiest hole on the card.
discovered_storylines.shape: At Penha Longa's 12th in R3, Jon ran up a 10 (b34) and Alex a 9 (b44), and neither stopped there: Jon dropped 11 shots across 11-13 with a quadruple 8 at the 13th (b21, b27), Alex dropped 12 across 11-14 without a net par in sight from the 12th (b19, b26). At Estoril in R4 the pattern simply moved along the card — Jon a quadruple-bogey 8 at the 11th, stroke index 2 (b36), Alex a septuple-bogey 11 at the 12th (b09). Two rounds, one hole number, one family: the 12th cost the brothers 15 shots over par between them in R3 alone.

vehicle_fit_response.note: Taken up as the comic engine — Alex Baker's blow-up inventory is genuinely inexhaustible — but it rides behind origin: the week belongs to Neumann's first Trophy after two Spoons and a 6th-5th-3rd-2nd climb.

why_the_champion_won: He built it himself: best in the field in R1, R2 and R3, never worse than 2nd of 5, and he beat Williams head-to-head in all four rounds — volatile from 35 to 43 points, but Williams playing to his own average still wouldn't have flipped the 13.
